questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with asthma presents with breathlessness. She is too breathless to complete sentences, RR 28, HR 122, PEF 42% predicted, SpO2 93% on room air.
questions.explanation: Severe: inability to complete sentences, PEF 33-50% predicted, RR ≥25, HR ≥110. Life-threatening requires PEF <33%, SpO2 <92%, silent chest, cyanosis, poor effort, exhaustion, altered consciousness, arrhythmia or hypotension — none present here. Near-fatal means a raised PaCO2 or need for ventilation. Her SpO2 of 93% sits just above the life-threatening threshold, which is the detail deciding this question.
questions.point: Severe asthma is PEF 33-50% predicted with inability to complete sentences; life-threatening requires PEF under 33% or SpO2 under 92%.

questions.stem: The same patient is treated with salbutamol and ipratropium nebulisers and oral prednisolone. An hour later she is quieter, drowsy, and her ABG shows pH 7.31, PaCO2 48mmHg (normal 35-45), PaO2 68mmHg.
questions.lead: How should the rising PaCO2 be interpreted?
options: Reassuring — she is settling and ventilating more normally
A sign of exhaustion and impending respiratory arrest
Evidence of a coexisting metabolic alkalosis
Suggests the diagnosis is not asthma
questions.explanation: An asthmatic in an acute attack should be hyperventilating with a LOW PaCO2. A normal or rising CO2 means she can no longer sustain the work of breathing — exhaustion and impending respiratory arrest. Combined with drowsiness and a quieter chest, this is near-fatal asthma requiring urgent ICU involvement. Mistaking the quieter chest and 'normalising' gas for improvement is the classic and lethal error.
questions.point: A normal or rising PaCO2 in acute asthma signals exhaustion and impending respiratory arrest, not improvement.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with COPD has an FEV1/FVC of 0.58 post-bronchodilator and FEV1 42% predicted. He has had two exacerbations needing oral steroids in the past year, neither requiring admission. His mMRC score is 2.
questions.explanation: FEV1 42% predicted falls in the 30-49% band = GOLD 3. Exacerbation history places him in Group E — under GOLD 2023 that required ≥2 moderate exacerbations or ≥1 hospitalisation, and GOLD has since lowered the threshold further. Group E overrides symptom score entirely, which is why mMRC 2 does not make him Group B. Group E is treated with LABA+LAMA, adding ICS if eosinophils ≥300.
questions.point: GOLD spirometric grade and exacerbation group are separate axes; Group E is determined by exacerbations regardless of symptom score.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old smoker has a 3-week history of cough with haemoptysis and 5kg weight loss. Sodium is 121 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality low, urine osmolality inappropriately high, and he is clinically euvolaemic.
questions.lead: What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Euvolaemic hyponatraemia with low serum and inappropriately concentrated urine is SIADH, and in a smoker with haemoptysis and weight loss the cause is small cell lung cancer — the classic SIADH-secreting tumour. Note the discriminator: squamous cell causes hyperCALCAEMIA via PTHrP, not hyponatraemia. Both are central tumours in smokers, and swapping the two paraneoplastic syndromes is the trap.
questions.point: Small cell lung cancer causes SIADH; squamous cell lung cancer causes hypercalcaemia via PTHrP.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness 10 days after a long-haul flight. She is haemodynamically stable, HR 102, SpO2 95%. Wells score is 4.5.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: A Wells score >4 makes PE likely, and in that group you proceed directly to CTPA — D-dimer is only useful to exclude PE in a low-probability patient, because a positive result in a high-probability patient changes nothing and a negative one cannot be trusted. V/Q is reserved for renal impairment, contrast allergy, or pregnancy where reducing breast radiation matters.
questions.point: With a Wells score above 4 the patient goes straight to CTPA; D-dimer is only for excluding PE in low-probability patients.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has progressive exertional breathlessness over 18 months and a dry cough. Examination shows fine bibasal inspiratory crackles and finger clubbing. Spirometry: FEV1 72% predicted, FVC 68% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.84. DLCO is reduced.
options: Restrictive disease — likely interstitial lung disease
questions.explanation: A preserved or raised FEV1/FVC ratio with both volumes reduced is the restrictive pattern; add reduced DLCO, fine bibasal crackles and clubbing and this is interstitial lung disease, most likely idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Obstruction would give a ratio <0.7. The ratio is what separates the two — reading only the absolute FEV1 is what misleads people here.
questions.point: Restrictive lung disease shows reduced FVC with a preserved or raised FEV1/FVC ratio.

questions.stem: A previously well 22-year-old tall thin man develops sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness. He is stable. CXR shows a 3cm rim of air at the level of the hilum with no mediastinal shift.
questions.lead: What is the most appropriate management?
options: Needle aspiration or small-bore chest drain
Immediate needle decompression at the 2nd intercostal space
questions.explanation: A primary spontaneous pneumothorax that is large (>2cm rim) or symptomatic is treated with aspiration or a small-bore drain. Small (<2cm) and asymptomatic pneumothoraces can be observed. Needle decompression is for tension pneumothorax, which this is not — he is stable with no mediastinal shift. Note the tall thin young male demographic is characteristic of primary spontaneous pneumothorax.
questions.point: A primary spontaneous pneumothorax over 2cm or symptomatic is aspirated; needle decompression is reserved for tension pneumothorax.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a pleural effusion. Pleural fluid protein is 38 g/L, serum protein 62 g/L. Pleural LDH 260 U/L, serum LDH 380 U/L.
questions.explanation: Apply Light's criteria — an effusion is an exudate if ANY one is met: pleural/serum protein >0.5 (here 38/62 = 0.61 ✓), pleural/serum LDH >0.6 (260/380 = 0.68 ✓), or pleural LDH >2/3 the upper limit of normal serum LDH. Two criteria are met, so this is an exudate — think malignancy, infection, PE, or inflammatory disease rather than heart failure or hypoalbuminaemia.
questions.point: Light's criteria define an exudate: pleural/serum protein above 0.5, or pleural/serum LDH above 0.6.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. He is confused, urea 8.2 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), RR 32, BP 88/56, age 58.
questions.lead: What is his CURB-65 score and what does it indicate?
questions.explanation: Confusion ✓, Urea >7 ✓, RR ≥30 ✓, BP systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60 ✓ (88/56 meets both), age 65 ✗ — he is 58. That gives 4. A score of 3 or more indicates severe pneumonia warranting admission and ICU assessment. The age criterion is the one most often misapplied: it is 65 and over, so a 58-year-old scores nothing for it.
questions.point: CURB-65 scores one point each for confusion, urea over 7, respiratory rate 30 or more, low BP, and age 65 or over.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with obesity reports daytime somnolence, unrefreshing sleep, and witnessed apnoeas. His wife describes loud snoring with pauses. He has resistant hypertension.
questions.explanation: Polysomnography (sleep study) confirms obstructive sleep apnoea and grades severity by the apnoea-hypopnoea index. STOP-BANG is a screening tool, not diagnostic. The association with resistant hypertension is worth knowing — OSA is a recognised secondary cause and should be considered in any patient whose blood pressure resists three agents. Treatment is CPAP plus weight loss, and it has implications for driving.
questions.point: Obstructive sleep apnoea is confirmed by polysomnography and is a recognised secondary cause of resistant hypertension.
